Heat pumps in winter: what homeowners need to know now

Post · 01 Jan 2026 4 min read

Contents

  1. Winter is an edge case, not the normal case
  2. COP is a snapshot, SPF is the arithmetic
  3. What should be measured before winter
  4. When the immersion heater takes over
  5. In closing

Simon Deussen

Founder & Managing Partner

A heat pump does not fail in summer. It fails on the twenty coldest days of the year, and what happens on those days is not in the data sheet — it is in the plant's own operating data, which is also where the reason for it is.

Winter is an edge case, not the normal case

The figures heat pumps are sold on are averages over a whole year. Winter is a small share of those hours and a large share of the work: in an average German house, roughly two thirds of the heat demand falls into four months. A system that runs cleanly in October therefore says very little about how it runs in February.

The reason is physics rather than product quality. The colder the outside air, the wider the gap between source and flow temperature, and the more electricity the same kilowatt-hour of heat costs. The relationship is well known and still rarely measured, because measuring it means recording two numbers at the same time that, in many installations, are produced in two different places.

COP is a snapshot, SPF is the arithmetic

COP describes one operating point: this much heat per kilowatt-hour of electricity, at this source temperature and this flow temperature. It is a number from a test bench. The seasonal performance factor is the same ratio over a full year of real operation — with defrost cycles, cycling losses, hot water and everything else that happens.

In practice the two are routinely a third apart. Anyone who wants to know what their system actually costs needs the second number, and it only comes from measuring over time: a heat meter on one side, and an electricity meter for the heat pump alone on the other. Without separate meters, every SPF is an estimate that happens to have a decimal place.

What should be measured before winter

Three quantities are enough to have an answer in spring instead of an opinion:

  • Flow temperature against outside temperature. The heating curve is the one setting that is too high in almost every installation. Each degree of flow temperature saved is roughly two and a half per cent of electricity.
  • Starts per day. Short, frequent starts are the most expensive operating state and the only one nobody notices without measuring. More than three starts an hour in mild weather points at a system that is oversized or set up wrong.
  • The immersion heater's share. It is the reserve for the coldest day, not the normal case. What it contributes over the year belongs in its own record — otherwise it disappears into the total, where nobody finds it again.

None of this needs new hardware. All of it needs the values that already exist to be recorded over the winter rather than merely displayed.

When the immersion heater takes over

The electric immersion heater is the point at which a heat pump stops being a heat pump: it turns one kilowatt-hour of electricity into one kilowatt-hour of heat, where the rest of the system makes three. That is correct at the design point and expensive spread across a winter.

What stands out is how often it runs for a reason other than the cold — a hot water setpoint left too high, a legionella cycle scheduled in the middle of a frost period, a screed-drying programme that was never switched off. Those are cases that take an hour to find in the data and years to pay for without it.

In closing

In winter the question is not whether the heat pump works — it works. The question is what it costs during the four months it does the work, and that is a question of measurement rather than of belief. Two meters and a recording are enough for a defensible answer in spring. Without them, the end of the heating season leaves an annual bill from which nobody can tell which kilowatt-hour was avoidable.
